query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor reactive sintering aid (e.g., approximately 1–2 wt% Ti) during a reactive spark plasma sintering (RSPS) process will promote localized alloying at the W/Cu interfaces, thereby forming a graded interphase that minimizes voids and phase separation while maintaining mechanical durability under fusion‐reactor irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite preform containing tungsten particles or an interconnected tungsten skeleton embedded within a copper matrix (fabricated by conventional powder metallurgy or infiltration methods)
generation.intervention: Reactive spark plasma sintering with a small addition of a sintering aid (Ti) incorporated into the mechanically alloyed W-Cu powder mixture
generation.conditions: Processing performed in an inert atmosphere at temperatures above the copper melting point but well below tungsten’s melting point, with further exposure to fusion-reactor relevant thermal cycling and irradiation conditions
generation.structural_mediator: A graded interfacial layer at the boundaries between tungsten and copper, resulting from localized alloying reactions induced by the sintering aid
generation.mechanism: The added Ti reacts preferentially at the W/Cu interface during RSPS to improve wetting and bonding, thereby reducing surface oxides and mitigating void formation and phase segregation. This creates a continuous and robust interphase that enhances both thermal transport and mechanical integrity
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional infiltration or non-reactive SPS methods, the RSPS with Ti additive will yield a W-Cu composite exhibiting lower porosity, a more uniform microstructure, improved thermal conductivity, and enhanced mechanical durability under irradiation
generation.baseline: W-Cu composites produced by standard spark plasma sintering or infiltration methods that typically experience interfacial void formation and phase separation
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable within processing temperature limits (copper molten, tungsten solid) and service conditions typical for fusion-reactor joint applications including cyclic thermal load and irradiation exposure
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration and choice of reactive sintering aid may require further experimental optimization, and the long-term stability of the graded interphase under extended irradiation remains to be fully established

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W-Cu composite samples: one using standard spark plasma sintering (baseline) and the other using reactive spark plasma sintering with ~1–2 wt% Ti as an additive. Subject both sample sets to identical processing schedules and then simulate fusion-reactor operating conditions involving thermal cycling and irradiation.
measurements: Microscopic analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess interfacial bonding and quantify porosity
EDS or XRD to characterize the formation of any graded interphase or intermetallic phases at the W/Cu boundary
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., tensile/compressive strength, cyclic fatigue) before and after simulated irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped RSPS samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in interfacial uniformity, porosity reduction, thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Abstract: AbstractAlloys with superior properties represent the main topic of recent studies due to their effectiveness in reducing the cost of equipment maintenance and enhancing usage time, in addition to other benefits in domains such as geothermal, marine, and airspace. Powder Metallurgy Processing of a WxTaTiVCr High-Entropy Alloy and Its Derivative Alloys for Fusion Material Applications

Abstract: The WxTaTiVCr high-entropy alloy with 32at.% of tungsten (W) and its derivative alloys with 42 to 90at.% of W with in-situ TiC were prepared via the mixing of elemental W, Ta, Ti, V and Cr powders followed by spark plasma sintering for the development of reduced-activation alloys for fusion plasma-facing materials. Characterization of the sintered samples revealed a BCC lattice and a multi-phase structure. The selected-area diffraction patterns confirmed the formation of TiC in the high-entropy alloy and its derivative alloys. It revealed the development of C15 (cubic) Laves phases as well in alloys with 71 to 90at.% W. A mechanical examination of the samples revealed a more than twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid-solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening. This study explored the potential of powder metallurgy processing for the fabrication of a high-entropy alloy and other derived compositions with enhanced hardness and strength.

Indentation Size Effect in CoCrFeMnNi HEA Prepared by Various Techniques

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are materials of great application potential and which have been extensively studied during the last two decades. As the number of possible element combinations is enormous, model materials representing certain groups of HEAs are used for the description of microstructure, properties, and deformation mechanisms. In this study, the microstructure and mechanical properties of the so-called Cantor alloy composed of Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni in equiatomic ratios prepared by various techniques (casting, melt-spinning, spark plasma sintering) were examined. The research focused on the indentation measurements, namely, the indentation size effect describing the evolution of the hardness with penetration depth. It was found that the standard Nix–Gao model can be used for this type of alloy at higher penetration depths and its parameters correlate well with microstructural observations. The Nix–Gao model deviates from the measured data at the submicrometer range and the applied modification affords additional information on the deformation mechanism.Keywords: CoCrFeMnNi, HEA,
